h1: Ranch Fencing Cost Per Foot: Real 2026 Numbers for Central Texas
heroSub: Straight answers on what fence really costs in McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties. Barbed wire from $2.50 a foot, pipe fence from $12, game fence from $4.50. Free written estimates and no guesswork.
introHtml:
Ask three contractors what ranch fencing costs per foot and you'll get three different answers. Here's the honest version: in 2026, most Central Texas ranch fence runs between $2.50 and $28 per foot depending on the fence type, your terrain, and how many corners and gates you need. A basic 5-strand barbed wire fence on flat pasture sits at the low end. A welded pipe fence along your road frontage sits at the top.

We build fence every week across Waco, China Spring, Crawford, and the rest of McLennan, Bosque, and Falls counties, so these numbers come from real jobs, not a national average. Below you'll find current per-foot and per-mile pricing for every fence type we install, plus the factors that push a bid up or down. When you're ready for an exact number, call (254) 555-0184 and we'll walk your line and put it in writing for free.

sections.heading: What Drives Your Price Per Foot
sections.html:
Two ranches a mile apart can get very different bids for the same fence, and it usually comes down to what's in the ground and what's on it. Here are the factors that move the number most:

  • Terrain and rock. Limestone and caliche are everywhere around Waco and the Bosque County hills. When we have to rock-drill post holes instead of augering them, labor goes up fast.
  • Brush clearing. A clean fence line is a cheap fence line. Heavy cedar or mesquite along the route can add $1 to $3 per foot before the first post goes in.
  • Corners, gates, and braces. Every corner and gate needs an H-brace or pipe corner. A square 10-acre tract has more corners per foot than a mile of straight perimeter, so short jobs cost more per foot.
  • Materials. Steel t-posts versus pipe line posts, standard barbed wire versus high-tensile game wire, drill stem versus new pipe. Material choice alone can double a bid.
  • Access and distance. Fence lines we can drive a truck along cost less than lines we have to carry material into by hand or side-by-side.

This is why we don't quote firm numbers over the phone. We walk the line first, then hand you a written estimate that won't grow on you later.

sections.heading: Cost by Fence Type: Which One Fits Your Operation
sections.html:
Barbed wire at $2.50 to $5.50 per foot is still the best value for cattle on larger acreage. If you're running goats or sheep, step up to net wire at $3.50 to $8 per foot so small stock stays put and coyotes stay out. Read more on our barbed wire fence page.

Pipe fence at $12 to $28 per foot costs more up front but it's the last fence you'll build on that line. Most of our customers use pipe fencing for road frontage, corrals, and working pens where cattle push hard, then run barbed wire on the back sections.

High game fence at $4.50 to $10 per foot is the standard for deer operations and exotics. On a per-mile basis figure $25,000 to $50,000 depending on clearing and terrain. Our game fence installation page covers heights, wire specs, and water gaps in detail.

Entrances and cattle guards finish the job. A custom ranch entrance runs $5,000 for a clean pipe entrance up to $25,000 and beyond for stone columns and overhead signage. An installed cattle guard runs $3,500 to $8,000 and pays for itself the first year you stop opening gates in the rain.

sections.heading: Budgeting a Big Job: Per-Mile Math That Actually Works
sections.html:
On tracts over 100 acres, think in miles, not feet. A mile is 5,280 feet, so barbed wire at $2.50 to $5.50 per foot pencils out to roughly $13,200 to $29,000 per mile, and 8-ft game fence lands between $25,000 and $50,000 per mile. Those ranges assume normal Central Texas conditions, some rock, some brush, a few water gaps.

Don't forget the extras that per-foot pricing leaves out: corner braces, gates, cattle guards, and clearing. On a typical perimeter job those items add 10 to 20 percent on top of the wire-and-post number. A good written estimate breaks all of it out line by line so there are no surprises, which is exactly how we quote every job from McGregor to West.

One more tip: fencing whole tracts at once almost always beats doing it in pieces. Mobilization, equipment hauling, and material delivery get spread over more feet, which drops your per-foot cost.

faq.q: How much does ranch fencing cost per foot in 2026?
faq.a: In Central Texas, most ranch fencing runs $2.50 to $28 per foot installed. Five-strand barbed wire is $2.50 to $5.50, net wire is $3.50 to $8, high game fence is $4.50 to $10, and welded pipe fence is $12 to $28 per foot. Terrain, brush, and the number of corners and gates decide where your job lands in those ranges.

faq.q: How much does it cost to fence one mile of ranch land?
faq.a: Figure roughly $13,200 to $29,000 per mile for 5-strand barbed wire and $25,000 to $50,000 per mile for 8-ft game fence. Add corner braces, gates, water gaps, and any cattle guards on top of that. Clearing heavy brush along the line is usually the biggest wildcard on per-mile pricing.

faq.q: What's the cheapest fence that will hold cattle?
faq.a: A properly built 5-strand barbed wire fence at $2.50 to $5.50 per foot is still the most cost-effective cattle fence there is. The key word is properly built. Good corner braces, tight wire, and posts set for your soil matter more than the wire itself. A cheap fence that lets cattle out onto a county road isn't cheap for long.

faq.q: Why is pipe fence so much more expensive than barbed wire?
faq.a: You're paying for steel and welding time. Pipe fence at $12 to $28 per foot uses far more material per foot, every joint is welded on site, and the posts are set in concrete. In return you get a fence that shrugs off cattle pressure, equipment bumps, and decades of weather. Most ranchers put pipe where it counts, like road frontage and pens, and run wire everywhere else.
